name: Grace Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the council's own home care team, not an agency, which people round here say is the good gig, though the pay's about the same. We cover the terraces on the hill above the old mill. I start at seven with Mr Lindqvist, who was a maths teacher and still corrects my sums when I count his tablets. Then it's five or six calls, a sandwich in the car outside the library, and four more in the afternoon. What wears me out is the lifting, my lower back's had it by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you keep track of everything during the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Printed rota in my bag and a notebook. The council gave us a tablet two years ago and I use it for the bare minimum, signing in and out. I don't do the AI thing at all, I've never even opened one of those chat apps. My partner Dev laughs at me, but he works in a warehouse that's full of scanners and I don't see him enjoying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So more or less what we've got now. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's always some big thing that's going to change the world, and then it doesn't. Care is people. I'd say that to anyone who asked, but I wouldn't post about it, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried about the council than about AI. There's been talk at the depot about handing home care to a private agency to save money, and if that happens our contracts go with it and the pay goes down. I've got maybe three weeks' money, and Dev's not much better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job well, so if they do outsource, I'm one they'd want to keep. I'd ask the union rep what happens to our contracts if the service is sold. And I'd stop the takeaways and put whatever's left at the end of the month in a pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried, not panicking. It's the usual background worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the service was handed to an agency, what would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sick pay, mainly. Agencies round here pay statutory sick pay and that's it. I did my back in two years ago and was off for three weeks on full pay. On an agency contract, three weeks off with my bad back would have wiped us out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving to an agency before it happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Why would I jump before I'm pushed? Better the devil you know. If it happens, I'll deal with it then.

say: I'd say there's always a **big thing** that doesn't change the world.
I'd tell people **care is people**, though I don't post online.
think: I worry more about the council **outsourcing home care** than about AI.
Outsourcing would mean **lower pay** and less **sick pay**, with three weeks' savings.
do: Keep her head down and **do the job well** to be kept on.
Ask the union rep what happens to **contracts if outsourced**.
Stop takeaways and put **leftover money** in a pot each month.
S0.quote: On an agency contract, three weeks off with my bad back would have wiped us out.
fieldNote: Her real worry is **council outsourcing**, a pressure that exists without AI.
She values **council sick pay** above everything after a back injury.
She refuses to **move before being pushed**, true to her resistant style.

steps.text: Keep doing her council rounds and avoid any complaints
Ask the union rep about contracts if the service is outsourced
Stop takeaways and save what's left each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work. So the council office, mostly. And the warehouses, I'd bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least nobody's built a robot that can get Mr Lindqvist into his trousers. I'd say care's going to be one of the safe jobs, and I'd probably say it a bit smugly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's Dev I'd worry about. My partner Dev's warehouse already has a trial with robot trolleys in one aisle, and if robots spread there first, he's out before I am. The council would also hand our rota to software, and I'd hate that, because our planner Gemma knows which clients can't cope with a new face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev to start looking now, maybe at the bus depot or the hospital. I'd learn whatever the tablet makes me learn and nothing else. And we'd cancel the car finance top-up we were planning, and keep the old car going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of relieved for me and knotted up for Dev. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn what the tablet makes you learn. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my job, yes. They don't need me to be a computer whizz to wash someone. If they ever do, I'll learn then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dev cut first if his hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His gym, then the Sky package. Then my mum's birthday weekend away, which would upset her more than him. We're not big spenders, so there isn't much to cut, that's the trouble.

say: I'd say care is one of the **safe jobs**, a bit smugly.
I'd joke that no robot can get a client **into his trousers**.
think: I'd worry about **Dev's warehouse**, which already trials robot trolleys.
Software running the rota would ignore what our **planner Gemma** knows.
do: Tell Dev to look now at the **bus depot or hospital**.
Learn only what the **council tablet** requires.
Cancel the planned **car finance top-up** and keep the old car.
feel: **Relieved** for herself and **knotted up** for Dev.
S1.quote: My partner Dev's warehouse already has a trial with robot trolleys in one aisle, and if robots spread there first, he's out before I am.
fieldNote: Her own job feels safe, but the **household income** is at risk through Dev.
She resists learning tech beyond **what's required**.
She'd miss **human planning** that knows clients, more than she fears software itself.

steps.text: Push Dev to apply at the bus depot or hospital now
Keep the old car and cancel the planned car finance top-up
Carry on her rounds, learning only what the tablet requires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That can't be right. And then robots by 2031?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say I don't believe it until I see it, and I'd mean it. Every few years someone says the robots are coming, and the buses still don't turn up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it was true, we'd be in real trouble. Dev's warehouse would go first, I'd guess before 2031, and the council would buy cheap robots for washing and dressing the minute they could, to save money. We've got three weeks' savings, and I don't know how to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do nothing in the first few months, I'll be honest, because I'd want to see it for myself. Once the council office started using it, I'd ask about the healthcare assistant jobs at the hospital, because hospitals might keep people longer. And we'd move in with my mum to save the rent, if Dev agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. And stupid, for not having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing for a few months. Is that the right call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. But I'm not someone who jumps. I'd wait until Gemma's rota got replaced, and then I'd know it was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most among your clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Kaur. My client Mrs Kaur is blind and knows me by my footsteps on her stairs. A robot wouldn't have footsteps she knew. I don't know what that does to someone.

say: I'd say **I don't believe it** until I see it.
I'd say people always claim **robots are coming**, and they don't.
think: I think **Dev's warehouse** would go first, before 2031.
The council would buy **cheap robots** for washing and dressing to save money.
With **three weeks' savings**, I don't know how to do anything else.
do: Wait a few months to see the **council office** change first.
Then ask about **healthcare assistant** jobs at the hospital.
Move in with her mum to **save rent**, if Dev agrees.
feel: **Sick** to her stomach, and stupid for having **no plan**.
S2.quote: My client Mrs Kaur is blind and knows me by my footsteps on her stairs. A robot wouldn't have footsteps she knew.
fieldNote: She **doubts the card** publicly but privately expects both incomes to go.
She'd **wait for proof** before acting, and admits that may be wrong.
Her fallback is **family**, moving in with her mum.

steps.text: Wait until the council rota is automated before acting
Apply for hospital healthcare assistant jobs once it's real
Move in with her mum to save rent if Dev agrees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least you'd see it coming down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said, that I'll believe it when I see it, but I'd say it a bit quieter. I'd probably tell people at the depot to keep their contracts safe and not sign anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the council would be slow, they always are, so I might get past 2034 before they actually buy robots. The council took six years to give us tablets, so I don't see them buying robots any faster. Dev's the one I'd worry about again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the council and start putting twenty-five a week aside, which would hurt. I'd make Dev do his forklift licence, because he's been putting it off. And I'd watch the news more, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the two-year one. More like a bad forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust the council to be slow. What if they aren't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be wrong and in trouble. But I've watched them for eight years. They took three years to fix the lift at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty-five a week: where from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lunches and the Sky package. Dev's not happy about Sky, but he'll live.

say: I'd say, more quietly, that **I'll believe it** when I see it.
I'd tell depot colleagues to **keep their contracts** and sign nothing new.
think: I think the **council would be slow** and might not buy robots before 2034.
**Dev's warehouse** job is again the bigger worry.
do: Keep her council job and **save twenty-five a week**.
Make Dev finally get his **forklift licence**.
Watch the **news more**, which she never does.
S3.quote: The council took six years to give us tablets, so I don't see them buying robots any faster.
fieldNote: Her hope rests on **council slowness**, based on eight years of watching it.
She'd start **saving** but still wouldn't change her own work.
Dev's job remains the **household weak point**.

steps.text: Save twenty-five a week by cutting lunches and Sky
Get Dev booked onto his forklift licence course
Stay on the council team and watch for robot purchases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, fine. I'd be thirty-seven, and the robots come when I'm forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people should calm down. I'd also say the government should make sure care workers aren't the last to be told what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's someone else's problem until the 2030s. The council won't have robots in my client Mr Lindqvist's bathroom before 2040, I'd bet money on it. Dev's warehouse might go earlier, but he'd have years to sort something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing much. I'd keep doing my rounds and keep the pot going. Maybe I'd let Dev show me the chat app, so I'm not completely lost later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. It's the money worry I always have, not this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really let Dev show you the chat app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. He's been trying for a year. If it means I can write a complaint to the council without it taking me an evening, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start planning seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing Gemma's rota go to a computer. That's my sign. Until then I've got clients to get up.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time**, so people should calm down.
I'd say care workers mustn't be the **last to be told**.
think: I think robots won't reach **council bathrooms** before 2040.
Dev would have **years to sort something** out, even if his warehouse goes earlier.
do: Keep doing her rounds and **keep the savings pot** going.
Maybe let Dev show her the **chat app**.
Start planning only when **Gemma's rota** goes to a computer.
feel: **Fine**, with only her usual money worry.
S4.quote: The council won't have robots in my client Mr Lindqvist's bathroom before 2040, I'd bet money on it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough for someone like me, I need to see things before I believe them, and by then it'd be too late. What would help is the council promising, in writing, that carers get first go at any new jobs, and that our contracts and sick pay stay put.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my back. Honestly, if a robot could do the heavy lifting and I did the talking, I'd take that tomorrow.

headlineQuote: If a robot could do the heavy lifting and I did the talking, I'd take that tomorrow.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old carer** on the council's in-house team in a former mill town.
She has **three weeks' savings** and values council sick pay after a back injury.
Her partner Dev works in a **warehouse trialling robots**, the household's weak point.
She avoids technology and would **wait for proof**, like the rota being automated, before acting.
She trusts that **council slowness** will protect her, more as the warning time grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd only believe it when it was too late.
whatWouldHelp: A written council promise of **first go** at new jobs.
A guarantee that **contracts and sick pay** stay put.
